artifacts.delta_brief: Change: In 2021, the risk narrative is still anchored in COVID-driven disruption and explicitly anticipates lingering sourcing constraints, with supply chain pressures expected to continue into 2022 (2021 para 7). By 2022, the emphasis broadens to macroeconomic conditions, especially inflation and commodity and energy price and supply shocks that can pressure liquidity and consumer demand (2022 para 1). 2022 also introduces the Russia and Ukraine conflict as a discrete multi-channel risk vector that can propagate through commodities, supply chains and cyber and workforce disruption (2022 para 9). Drivers: The operating threat model shifts from pandemic channel mix volatility to affordability and input-cost mechanics, where broad economic tightening and commodity swings become the main transmission path (2022 para 1) alongside still-relevant supply chain strain (2021 para 7). The conflict narrative widens the tail by layering sanctions and geopolitical disruption onto core cost and availability risks and by explicitly calling out cyber incident risk tied to the conflict environment (2022 para 9). In parallel, KO elevates data governance as an operating constraint, warning that expanding regulation of data practices can raise compliance cost and limit growth (2022 para 108). Caveat: Longer-horizon regulatory and reputation risks persist, including health-perception driven regulation and labeling risk that can translate into taxes, negative publicity and demand erosion (2021 para 50). Execution and disclosure risk around ESG commitments also remains, with outcomes dependent on bottlers, suppliers and other third parties outside KO control (2021 para 118).

evidence.snippet: Although we are unable to predict the impact on our ability to source materials in the future, we expect supply chain pressures to continue into 2022.
evidence.why: Shows 2021 framing that COVID-era sourcing and logistics constraints remain a near-term operating risk and are expected to spill into 2022.

evidence.snippet: In addition, increasing public concern about actual or perceived health consequences of the presence of such ingredients or substances in our beverage products or in packaging materials, whether or not justified, could result in additional governmental regulations concerning the advertising, marketing, labeling, packaging or sale of our beverages;
evidence.why: Captures the mechanism where consumer health perceptions can trigger regulation and labeling constraints, creating demand and reputational downside beyond pure cost shocks.

evidence.snippet: Our ability to achieve our ESG goals and objectives and to accurately and transparently report our progress presents numerous operational, financial, legal and other risks, and are dependent on the actions of our bottling partners, suppliers and other third parties, all of which are outside of our control.
evidence.why: Establishes that ESG delivery and reporting are treated as operational and legal risk, with dependency on bottlers and suppliers limiting control over outcomes.

evidence.snippet: changes in global economic conditions, including inflation, credit market conditions, increased unemployment, levels of consumer and business confidence, commodity (including energy) prices and supply, a recession or economic slowdown, trade policies, foreign currency exchange rates
evidence.why: Signals a 2022 pivot toward broad macro drivers like inflation, unemployment and commodity supply and pricing as the core channels affecting liquidity and performance.

evidence.snippet: the conflict has resulted, and could continue to result, in volatile commodity markets, supply chain disruptions, increased risk of cyber incidents or other disruptions to our information systems, reputational risk, heightened risks to employee safety, business disruptions (including labor shortages)
evidence.why: Adds a conflict-specific risk bundle that links geopolitical events to commodities, supply chains and cyber and labor disruption, expanding the tail of operational shocks.

evidence.snippet: Increased regulation of data collection, use, disclosure and retention practices, including self-regulation and industry standards, changes in existing laws and regulations, enactment of new laws and regulations, increased enforcement activity, and changes in interpretation of laws, could increase our cost of compliance and operation
evidence.why: Introduces explicit data regulation and enforcement as a cost and growth constraint, complementing the shift from pandemic framing to structural compliance and operating friction.

warnings: Focuspack is a subset; verify in full compare pane.
Narrative shifts may reflect risk-factor reorganization as well as changes in underlying exposure.
